topic.title: Rs 99 sells permission, not food
topic.claim: The Rs 99 meal works because it removes the guilt, not because it is a bargain.
topic.behaviour: You order in when you are tired, and a Rs 99 tag turns a lazy decision into a sensible one.
topic.mechanism: A low fixed price makes ordering feel safe. Apps use it to bring back users who stopped ordering, and they spend heavily on pricing to do it.
topic.group: Young professionals who order in because they are tired, not hungry
topic.moment: It is 9 pm, you are done with the day, and the Rs 99 meal makes ordering feel responsible.

turn.believed: You order because the food is cheap.
turn.actually: You order because the price silences the voice that says you could cook.

topic.feeling: Relieved and slightly guilty at the same time
topic.villain: A discount model built to win back lapsed users
topic.because: Apps earn on frequency, not on one meal. A low price pulls back people who stopped ordering and makes ordering a habit again.

proof.fact: Swiggy says its Bolt and ₹99 Store offers together made up over 25% of food-delivery volumes, and that Instamart's losses peaked this quarter after it spent on pricing to win back dormant users.

topic.payoff: Ask yourself on the next order: am I hungry, or just tired and given permission?
topic.send_to: The friend who says they order in 'only when the offer is good'
real_details: Its affordable-meals app Toing, now in 50+ cities, is drawing mostly new or long-inactive users.
topic.news_peg: Swiggy's Q2 results on 22 October 2026 showed Bolt and ₹99 Store offers made up over 25% of food-delivery volumes.
topic.why_now: Festive-season ordering is up and the cheap-meal offer is now a big part of the app's volume.

score.why: The Rs 99 meal removes the guilt of not cooking; 'hungry or just given permission' is the self-test.
